slides.title: Mediated Sign-In
slides.subtitle: Relay the user's credentials to one company endpoint, once, out of the model's sight
slides.notes: Some companies cannot send their users to a browser. With Mediated Sign-In, the personal agent relays what the user types to the company. The example runs the real MediatedSignInClient against Manzanita Outfitters, which asks for an email, a password, and then a one-time code.

slides.title: Why it needs care
slides.statement: The one sign-in mode where a **password** passes through the host. So the SDK **narrows** what the host can do with it.
slides.notes: In every other mode the company's own page takes the password. Here it passes through the agent's host, so the SDK limits where it can go, how often, and who can see it. The protocol calls Mediated Sign-In transitional: for companies that cannot offer Direct or Device Sign-In yet, and meant to be removed, as OAuth 2.1 removed the password grant.

never the chat"] -- "values" --> S["MediatedSignInClient
sends once, drops"] S -- "tokens" --> V[("Reactor stores")] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB C["Mediated endpoint
on its own domain"] end USR -- "types credentials, code" --> HOST HOST -- "one POST with DPoP" --> CO HOST -. "labels, domain, masked sent_to" .-> M
slides.caption: The password crosses the host once, to the company's own domain, and never reaches the model.
slides.notes: Start with the user, who types the email, the password and later the code into pap.protectedInput, the host's trusted surface, never the chat. The MediatedSignInClient sends those values once, in one POST with a DPoP proof, to the endpoint the company declared on its own domain, then drops them. The tokens that come back go into Reactor stores. Off to the side, the model: it knows the field labels and which are secret, the company's domain, where the code was sent, masked, and the statuses and granted scopes. That is enough to guide the user, and none of it is a value.

slides.title: Credentials, then a code

items.title: Check
items.detail: Endpoint on the company's domain, or refuse

items.title: Ask
items.detail: Email and password, in protected input

items.title: Send once
items.detail: POST with DPoP, no redirect followed; values dropped

slides.notes: The client checks the endpoint before asking the user anything. It sends the credentials once, with a DPoP proof, follows no redirect, and drops the values. The company asks for a code sent to a masked address; the user types it, the code goes only to that sign-in, and the Session comes back signed in.

slides.title: The sign-in, with its refusals
slides.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Signed out" as SO
  state "Refused" as RF
  state "Code required" as CR
  state "Complete" as OK
  state "Failed" as FL
  [*] --> SO
  SO --> RF : endpoint off domain
  SO --> CR : credentials sent once
  CR --> CR : wrong code
  CR --> OK : right code
  CR --> FL : attempt limit
slides.caption: Every refusal is a state the host can explain; only the right code from the right Session completes.
slides.notes: Start signed out. If the declared endpoint is off the company's domain, the client refuses with unsafe_mediated_endpoint before the user is asked anything. Otherwise the credentials go once, and the company answers code_required. A wrong code comes back as code_required again, with the same reference. The right code completes the sign-in. After its own attempt limit, the company answers failed. Two more refusals do not change the state: the protected input must answer exactly the declared fields, none empty, and only the Session that started the sign-in can finish it; any other Session, under another Session Key, gets session_mismatch, and the pending state is kept for the right one.

slides.title: What stays where

left.heading: Never the model's
items: Credentials and the code: protected input and one request body
Session Token and Account Token: Reactor stores

right.heading: What the model sees
items: Field labels, and which are secret

slides.notes: The model knows enough to guide the user: which fields, which company, where the code went. The values themselves exist only in the protected input and in the single request that carries them.

slides.title: In TypeScript
slides.notes: TypeScript has the same client. The trusted input surface is contributed at the ProtectedInputs contribution point.
